mainEntity.name: Why is −7 mod 3 equal to 2, not −1?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under the mathematical (floored) convention, the result of a mod n always has the same sign as n (here positive), so it stays in [0, n). −7 = 3 × (−3) + 2, giving remainder 2. Some programming languages instead truncate toward zero, giving −1 — this calculator shows both.

mainEntity.name: When does a modular inverse not exist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exactly when gcd(a, n) ≠ 1 — that is, a and n share a common factor. For example, 4 has no inverse mod 8, since gcd(4, 8) = 4.

mainEntity.name: How is aᵇ mod n computed for a huge exponent b?

acceptedAnswer.text: By fast (binary) exponentiation: repeatedly squaring a mod n and multiplying in the factors corresponding to the binary digits of b, taking the modulus at every step. This needs only about log₂(b) multiplications, so even a 1000-digit exponent computes instantly.

mainEntity.name: What is the modulo operation used for?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clock and calendar arithmetic, hash tables, checksums, cryptography (RSA relies on modular exponentiation), pseudo-random number generators, and cycling through array indices.

mainEntity.name: How is congruence different from equality?

acceptedAnswer.text: Equality means two numbers are identical. Congruence mod n is weaker: it only requires them to leave the same remainder when divided by n, so infinitely many numbers (…, b−n, b, b+n, b+2n, …) are all congruent to b.
